notes.short: A crown set on Joshua the high priest
notes.about: Zechariah is told to take silver and gold from exiles come from Babylon, make a crown and set it on the head of Joshua the high priest. The next words explain the act: the Branch will build the LORD's temple and be a priest on His throne. It foretells the Messiah, both priest and king.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: make an ornate crown, and set it on the head of the high priest
figure.means: the Branch to come, who joins the king's office to the priest's: He will build the LORD's temple and rule as a priest on His throne

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry says the prophet here speaks by a sign many saw, foretelling the Messiah as priest and king of His church. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) calls it a symbolic act: a royal crown on the high priest shows that He whom priests stood for would also be King. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the crowning was typical, pointing to one who joins kingship and priesthood in himself.
notes.limit: One writer leaves open whether the prophet carried out the act outwardly.

cites.quote: In the former part of this chapter he spoke by a vision, which only the prophet himself saw; here, in this latter part, he speaks by a sign, or type, which many saw, and which, as it was explained, was an illustrious prediction of the Messiah as the priest and king of his church.

In any case the symbolical act was completed by the placing of a royal crown upon the head of the high priest. This, in itself, represented that He, whom he and all other priests represented, would be also our King.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The crowning of Joshua the high priest with a royal crown ... had a typical significance. It pointed to a man who would sit upon his throne as both ruler and priest ... The question whether the prophet really carried out the symbolical action enjoined upon him in Zac 6:10 ., externally or not, can neither be answered in the affirmative nor with a decided negative.

notes.short: Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, then back to Ashkelon
notes.about: Three cities are named, Ashkelon, Gaza and Ekron, and then taken up in reverse: Ekron's hope will wither, Gaza will lose its king, and Ashkelon will be uninhabited.

lines.words: There will cease to be a king in Gaza,

notes.evidence: Boys gives the verse as an introverted arrangement of six members: Ashkelon in the first and last, Gaza in the second and fifth, Ekron in the third and fourth.

cites.quote: The instances of introverted arrangement which have hitherto been given in the present work, consist of no more than four members each. There are, however, similar ones of six members, or more. … Here we have Ashkelon in a. and a., Gaza in b. and b., Ekron in c. and c.

notes.short: The shepherd who breaks his staffs Favor and Union
notes.about: The prophet is told to shepherd a flock marked for slaughter. He takes two staffs, Favor and Union. He breaks Favor, is paid thirty pieces of silver and throws them to the potter, then breaks Union. He stands for the Lord Himself as Shepherd, come in Christ, whom the flock rejects.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: Then I took for myself two staffs, calling one Favor and the other Union
figure.means: the Lord's own care for His people as their Shepherd; breaking the staffs takes away His favor and the brotherhood of Judah and Israel, once they reject Him

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a symbolical act, seen in vision, showing the Lord's care for His people. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the prophet acts as representing Another, our Lord. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says Zechariah acts in vision as a type of Messiah. Matthew Henry makes the prophet a type of Christ and the broken staff a sign of the broken covenant.
notes.limit: Two of the writers place these acts in a vision rather than in outward deeds.

cites.quote: This section contains a symbolical act. By the command of Jehovah the prophet assumes the office of a shepherd over the flock, and feeds it, until he is compelled by its ingratitude to break his shepherd's staff ... as an internal occurrence of a visionary character and of prophetical importance, through which the faithful care of the Lord for His people is symbolized and exhibited.

cites.quote: The fulfillment of the whole prophecy shows, that the person addressed is the prophet, not in, or for himself, but (as belongs to symbolic prophecy) as representing Another, our Lord. ... But He, the Shepherd addressed, who does the acts commanded, speaks with the authority of God.

cites.quote: Zechariah here represents typically Messiah, and performs in vision the actions enjoined: hence the language is in part appropriate to him, but mainly to the Antitype, Messiah. ... The typical breaking of the staff, performed in vision by Zechariah ( Zac 11:10 ), is fulfilled in His breaking the covenant with Judah.

cites.quote: The prophet here is made a type of Christ, as the prophet Isaiah sometimes was ... A sign of it given ... in token of this, that he would be no longer a shepherd to them ... The breaking of this staff signified the breaking of God's covenant which he had made with all the people

notes.short: The prophet takes up a foolish shepherd's gear
notes.about: With the good shepherd rejected, the prophet is told to take up a foolish shepherd's gear. The next words explain the act: God will raise up a shepherd who neglects and devours the flock, and woe will fall on him. The flock that refused its good shepherd gets a worthless one.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: Take up once more the equipment of a foolish shepherd
figure.means: the worthless ruler God would set over the flock that rejected its true Shepherd, one who devours the sheep instead of caring for them

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a new symbolical action, its meaning given in the next verse: Israel, having driven off the good shepherd, is given to a foolish one. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the prophet plays a bad shepherd, as before a good one, as the people would not have Messiah. Matthew Henry says the prophet represents the foolish shepherd set over them.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whom the foolish shepherd stands for: the Roman power, the people's own unfaithful teachers, or a false ruler still to come.

cites.quote: After Israel has compelled the good shepherd to lay down his shepherd's office, in consequence of its own sin, it is not to be left to itself, but to be given into the hand of a foolish shepherd, who will destroy it. ... The reason for the divine command is given in Zac 11:16 by a statement of the meaning of the new symbolical action.

cites.quote: Assume the character of a bad ("foolish" in Scripture is synonymous with wicked, Psa 14:1 ) shepherd, as before thou assumedst that of a good shepherd. Since the Jews would not have Messiah, "the Good Shepherd" ( Joh 10:11 ), they were given up to Rome ... and shall be again to Antichrist, the "man of sin," the instrument of judgment by Christ's permission.

cites.quote: God, having shown the misery of this people in their being justly abandoned by the good Shepherd, here shows their further misery in being shamefully abused by a foolish shepherd. The prophet is himself to personate and represent this pretended shepherd ... for such a shepherd shall be set over them ... They shall be under the inspection of unfaithful ministers.
